classification.summary: Insufficient abstract to determine whether placebo was analyzed as an object of study; trial compared EMG biofeedback, verbal relaxation, and a medication placebo for tension headaches.

title: Letter: The placebo effect.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the letter's main subject is the placebo effect and it is a substantive editorial/letter about placebo science.

classification.summary: Was a letter in JAMA discussing the placebo effect; full text not available in the record.

title: Management of muscle cramps in hemodialysis patients. Controlled prospective study.
journal: Proceedings of the Clinical Dialysis and Transplant Forum
abstract: In conclusion, a blind, prospective study demonstrated that HS was the most effective way of treating muscle cramps induced by hemodialysis. Hypertonic non-electrolyte solutions were less effective. The chance of a placebo effect in these patients is about 13.0%.

screening.rationale: Abstract reports a blind controlled trial and gives a placebo-effect 'chance' (13%), but the summary does not make clear whether the paper analyzed placebo/placebo-arm responses as an object of study or merely reported a comparator rate.

classification.summary: Reported a blind, prospective controlled trial in hemodialysis patients finding hypertonic saline most effective for dialysis-induced muscle cramps and noting a ~13% chance of a placebo effect.

title: The effect of multiple intramuscular placebo injections on injection-site tolerance and serum creatine phosphokinase activity.
journal: Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental

screening.rationale: Empirical controlled clinical trial whose stated aim concerned effects of intramuscular placebo injections on local tolerance and serum CPK.

classification.summary: Tested effects of multiple intramuscular placebo injections on injection-site tolerance and serum creatine phosphokinase in adult men in a controlled clinical trial.

title: Correlates of placebo reaction in an outpatient population.
abstract: Variables describing 113 outpatients of a mental health clinic were derived from a Placebo Test, the MMPI, a Symptom Check List, measures a response style, and a questionnaire containing historical and demographic information. Two highly reliable scales, the Placebo Effect Scale (PES) and the Side Effect Scale (SES) were derived from the Placebo Test and served as dependent variables. PES scores were inversely related to reporting symptoms and unrelated to measures of response style. SES scores were directly related to reporting symptoms and with several measures of response style. There was a curvilinear relationship between placebo response and reporting side effects. Implications of results for further research are presented.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that explicitly analyzed placebo reaction (Placebo Effect Scale) and side-effect reporting in an outpatient clinical sample.

classification.summary: Analyzed correlates of placebo and side-effect responding in 113 mental-health outpatients using a Placebo Test, MMPI, and symptom measures, finding distinct predictors for placebo-response and side-effect reporting.
classification.key_finding: Placebo-effect scores were inversely related to symptom reporting while side-effect scores were positively related to symptom reporting and response-style measures.

title: Effects of "natural oestrogen" replacement therapy on menopausal symptoms and blood clotting.
abstract: In a double-blind study on the value of equine ("natural") oestrogens 30 patients presenting with menopausal symptoms in a group practice were monitored for possible adverse effects on blood clotting, weight, and blood pressure. The women were randomly allocated to two groups and given either three months' hormone treatment followed by three months' placebo or vice versa. An appreciable amelioration of all symptoms on placebo made it difficult to asses the genuine value of oestrogen treatment during the period of study. Both groups made a dramatic clinical improvement during the first three months. Nevertheless, the symptoms of the 15 women who received oestrogen first returned after the cross-over to placebo without any suggestion of a placebo response. In contrast, the other group who took placebo first did not deteriorate after changing to oestrogen. The menopausal index and the karyopyknotic index were not reliable guides to the need for oestrogen treatment. Hot flushes, however, were proportionately reduced on oestrogen and they seemed to be more readily eliminated in individual cases by oestrogen. The results of blood clotting studies indicated that natural oestrogen administration raised the levels of the extrinsic clotting factors VII and X and accelerated the prothrombin time. The findings were similar to those observed after three months synthetic oestrogen administration with oral contraception. Long-term studies and epidemiological surveys of the clinical incidence of thrombotic and other sequelae are needed before large-scale oestrogen replacement treatment can be recommended.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial that reported and discussed substantial placebo-arm improvement (placebo response) as a central analytic issue rather than using placebo solely as an efficacy comparator.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial of equine oestrogen versus placebo in 30 menopausal women found marked symptom improvement on placebo and oestrogen-specific reductions in hot flushes plus changes in clotting factors.
classification.key_finding: Found large placebo-arm symptom improvement complicating efficacy estimates; oestrogen reduced hot flushes and increased clotting factors VII and X and accelerated prothrombin time.

title: Psychopharmacologic investigations in elderly volunteers: Effect of diazepam in males.
journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
abstract: Forty male volunteers over the age of 60 took either a daily dose of diazepam (12 mg) or placebo for a two-week period. Differential responses to these compounds partially depended upon age and the initial symptom level. Diazepam produced sedative side effects, a modest antidepressant effect, and a reduction in memory. Placebo had an antianxiety effect in the relatively older subjects, and was associated with decreased fatique, improved memory and improved motor function. Considerable variability was observed in both drug and placebo responses among the elderly. A self-rating depression scale (D30R) was useful for assessing changes in affective states and in discriminating between the effects of active drug and placebo.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial reported and analyzed placebo-arm responses (antianxiety, reduced fatigue, improved memory and motor function) so placebo response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized trial in 40 men over 60 compared diazepam versus inert pill and found placebo produced antianxiety effects and improved fatigue, memory, and motor function in older subjects.
classification.key_finding: Placebo produced measurable subjective and objective improvements (antianxiety, less fatigue, better memory and motor function) in elderly male volunteers.

title: A clinical trial design avoiding undue placebo treatment.
abstract: A design is descirbed of a modified placebo-controlled double-blind clinical trial procedure. The design was evolved in attempt to overcome certain problems inherent in the conventional double-blind procedure, in particular the ethical problem of prolonged exposure of the patient to placebo treatment. The modified designs consist of two phases. In the first (open) phase, patients selected according to the normal protocol requirements are given the medication under study for a predetermined time. Patients responding favorably to such treatment then enter a second (double blind) phase during which is tested the null hypothesis that all the favorable effects observed during the open phase are placebo effects. Experience with this clinical trial design in the evaluation of an antianginal agent is briefly described. In this case, the null hypothesis was disproved, and a potent therapeutic action was evidenced.

screening.rationale: Paper primarily described and evaluated a modified clinical-trial design to address ethical and methodological issues of placebo exposure, meeting inclusion for placebo-related trial methodology.

classification.summary: Described a two-phase trial design (open active treatment run-in then double-blind phase) intended to minimize undue prolonged placebo exposure and illustrated it using an antianginal (lidoflazine) evaluation.
classification.key_finding: Applied design to an antianginal trial and found the open-phase effects were not attributable to placebo, supporting a therapeutic action of the drug.

title: Clonidine in menopausal flushing: a double-blind trial.
abstract: Twelve hypertensive women were treated with low doses of the antihypertensive drug clonidine for their menopausal flushing in a double-blind trial. There was a high degree of placebo effect but clonidine at a daily dose of 150mug was more effective than placebo.

screening.rationale: Double-blind randomized trial reported a substantial placebo effect and compared placebo arm response versus active clonidine, so placebo response was an analyzed finding.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind randomized trial in 12 hypertensive menopausal women and found a high placebo response, though clonidine 150 µg/day reduced flushing more than placebo.
classification.key_finding: Found a substantial placebo response but clonidine produced greater reduction in menopausal flushing than placebo in this small trial.

title: A study of metaxalone (Skelaxin) vs. placebo in acute musculoskeletal disorders: a cooperative study.
journal: Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental

screening.rationale: Title indicates a placebo-controlled drug efficacy RCT but no abstract or full text was available to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or responses rather than drug efficacy.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a randomized controlled comparison of metaxalone (Skelaxin) versus placebo for acute musculoskeletal disorders in humans.

title: Follow-up of empirically obtained groups of psychotic patients and their placebo response.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly states follow-up of psychotic patient groups and their placebo response, indicating the placebo response was an object of study despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: Followed empirically obtained groups of psychotic patients and reported on their placebo response during follow-up.

title: Human assay of antimotion sickness drugs.
abstract: The present study was undertaken to improve previous testing procedures, involving the use of a slow rotation room, for assessing the efficacy of antimotion sickness drugs which had validity for groups of subjects but not for each individual in the group. Three major changes were introduced: first, the use of an incremental increase in the intensity of the stressful stimuli of constant intensity; second, a systematic distribution of placebos, rather than a random distribution, in using a modified Latin-square design; third, categorizing the responses as "inconsquential," "beneficial," and "detrimental"--the range of the "placebo responses" was doubled to define the inconsequential range and response above or below were, respectively, beneficial or detrimental. Only drugs known to have antimotion sickness effectiveness were tested and the cardinal findings can be briefly summarized: 1) The group responses were similar to the data previously reported; 2) Great individual differences in response to antimotion sickness drugs were revealed, implying that individual assessments must be made for maximal benefits; 3) The fixed-dose combination of promethazine hydrochloride and ephedrine sulfate (25 mg each) proved to be outstanding as this combination of homergic drugs clearly exhibited a suprasummation effect; and 4) A few tests were conducted using larger than usual doses and the results supported previous findings that, for a maximal beneficial effect in response to a single dose, individuals may vary both with regard to the choice of drug and the amount administered.

screening.rationale: Clinical trial explicitly manipulated and characterized placebo responses (systematic distribution of placebos and categorization of placebo response), meeting inclusion for placebo_response.

classification.summary: Tested known antimotion-sickness drugs in a slow-rotation assay with systematic placebo distribution and classified placebo responses, finding large individual differences and variable placebo effects.
classification.key_finding: Found large individual variability in placebo responses and that promethazine+ephedrine produced suprasummation; individuals varied in optimal drug and dose.

title: Evaluation of baclofen (Lioresal) for spasticity in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: The effect of baclofen on spasticity and muscle spasms was assessed in thirty-five patients with multiple sclerosis. Benefit from reduction of spasticity was obtained in sixteen patients. A higher proportion of patients confined to a wheelchair was helped than ambulant patients, but overall functional improvement was limited. Twenty-one of the thirty-five patients had troublesome spasms and thirteen of them had significant relief on baclofen. Substituting identical dummy tablets confirmed that benefit was attributable to the pharmacological effects of baclofen in ten of the sixteen patients whose spasticity was reduced and in eight of the thirteen whose muscle spasms were relieved. In two of the remainder, benefit appeared to be due to placebo effect, and the others maintained their improvement after stopping the drug. The drug had to be withdrawn in nine patients because of increased weakness and in ten other patients who had intolerable side effects. The optimum dose of baclofen tolerated ranged from 15 mg to 80 mg daily. The importance of adjusting the dose regime to the requirement of each individual and starting with small doses in multiple sclerosis is emphasized.

screening.rationale: Empirical clinical trial that substituted identical dummy tablets to attribute improvement to pharmacologic versus placebo effects, so placebo effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Conducted in 35 MS patients, baclofen reduced spasticity in 16 and dummy-tablet substitution indicated pharmacologic benefit in 10 patients and probable placebo benefit in 2, with frequent side effects prompting withdrawal in several patients.
classification.key_finding: Dummy-tablet substitution confirmed drug-specific benefit in 10/16 improved patients and suggested placebo-attributable improvement in 2 patients.

title: Problem-solving training groups for hospitalized psychiatric patients.
abstract: Small groups lasting eight sessions each and aimed at improving patient's interpersonal problem-solving skills were conducted for a total of 41 hospitalized psychiatric patients. Forty control patients received the same pre and posttests but notraining. Twenty-three patients participated in play-reading groups without problem-solving training (placebo condition). Three separate 3 by 2 repeated measures analyses of variance showed that hospitalization alone improved the patient's functioning on the criterion test of problem-solving, but the problem-solving training groups advanced the improvement significantly. More disturbed patients made only slightly greater gains than less disturbed ones. The hospital stay was significantly shorter for the experimental and the placebo groups than for the control sample.

screening.rationale: Empirical controlled clinical trial that included an explicit placebo (play‑reading) psychological condition and reported effects of that placebo on outcomes (length of stay) and functioning.

classification.summary: Conducted controlled group trial in hospitalized psychiatric patients comparing problem-solving training, play-reading (placebo), and control, and found training improved problem-solving and both training and placebo groups had shorter hospital stays.
classification.key_finding: Both the active problem-solving groups and the play-reading placebo groups had significantly shorter hospital stays than controls, and training produced greater gains on problem‑solving tests.

title: Amoxapine, imipramine and placebo in depressive illness.
journal: Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and the trial appears to be a standard drug efficacy RCT with placebo as a comparator, so it is unclear whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses as an object of study.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to determine whether the trial analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or responses; reported as a comparative clinical trial of amoxapine, imipramine, and placebo in depression.

title: Attribution theory, insomnia, and the reverse placebo effect: a reversal of Storms and Nisbett's findings.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: Storms and Nisbett found that insomniacs got to sleep faster than usual on nights when they took placebos believed to be arousal pills. Our study attempted: (a) to replicate the reverse placebo effect using a method of measurement considered more accurate than the original technique, (b) to evaluate the effect of an arousal pill therapy after therapy is discontinued, and (c) to clarify which of two hypotheses better accounts for the effect. Using 42 insomniacs, the design varied whether pills were administered (pill) or withheld (no pill) and whether or not high justification was provided for taking the pills. The high-justification-pill and the high-justification-no-pill groups were given information intended to justify their participation, while the no-justification-pill and no-pill-no-justification groups were treated like the original arousal and control groups. Instead of a decrease in latency to sleep, the no-justification-pill group but not the high-justification-pill troup displayed a typical placebo reaction on nights they took the pills. Our results cast suspicion on the original finding. The lack of response by the high-justification-pill group is discussed in terms of Bem and Kelley's views of attribution theory.

screening.rationale: Empirical controlled trial that manipulated pill vs no-pill and examined placebo (reverse placebo) effects on insomnia sleep latency, so the placebo effect was the object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized groups of 42 insomniacs received pills or no pills with high- or no-justification; the no-justification-pill group showed a typical placebo (reduced sleep latency) while the high-justification-pill group did not.
classification.key_finding: No-justification-pill participants showed a placebo-related decrease in sleep latency on pill nights, whereas high-justification participants did not.

title: Anorectic effectiveness of various dosages of fenfluramine and placebo: a cooperative study.
journal: Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates an RCT comparing fenfluramine dosages with placebo (placebo likely served as a control for drug efficacy) but it's unclear whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses as an object of study.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported as a controlled clinical trial comparing various fenfluramine dosages with placebo for anorectic (weight-loss) effects, but text did not indicate whether placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses were analyzed.

title: The placebo effect in podiatry.
journal: Journal of the American Podiatry Association

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses the placebo effect in podiatry and publication types indicate an RCT addressing postoperative pain with placebos, meeting inclusion as a study of placebo effects in a clinical context despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: No abstract available; paper title and indexing indicated a randomized trial addressing the placebo effect for postoperative foot pain in podiatry.

title: Effects of marihuana and placebo marihuana smoking on hemodynamics in coronary disease.

screening.rationale: Clinical trial explicitly compared marihuana and placebo-marihuana smoking effects on hemodynamics in coronary disease, so placebo/sham treatment was the object of study.

classification.summary: Compared marihuana and placebo-marihuana smoking on hemodynamic outcomes in patients with coronary disease.

title: The placebo effect. A neglected asset in the care of patients.

screening.rationale: Title and journal indicate the paper is a conceptual/commentary focused on the placebo effect as an aspect of clinical care, meeting inclusion for placebo science commentary despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses the placebo effect as an underused clinical asset and its relevance to physician–patient interaction and patient care.

title: Psychopharmacologic investigations in healthy elderly volunteers: effects of pipradrol-vitamin (Alertonic) elixir and placebo in relation to research design.
journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
abstract: Ninety-nine healthy elderly volunteers were tested to assess the effects of: 1) a pipradrol-vitamin (Alertonic) elixir, 2) a placebo, and 3) no treatment, during a one-week period. The assessment measures were the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory Depression Scale, the Zung Depression Scale, Profile of Mood States, and the WAIS Digit Span. Alertonic had no sigmificant effects on mood, memory or appetite, and the placebo effect was rarely greater than 50 per cent. There were no significant side effects. The findings demonstrate a valid method for studying psychotropic agents in the elderly.

screening.rationale: Three-arm trial included a placebo and no-treatment arm and explicitly reported placebo effects, allowing estimation of placebo effect versus no treatment.

classification.summary: Randomized trial in 99 healthy elderly volunteers compared Alertonic elixir, placebo, and no treatment for one week and found no significant effects on mood, memory, or appetite and minimal placebo responses.
classification.key_finding: Found no significant placebo or drug effects on mood (MMPI Zung POMS) or memory (WAIS digit span); placebo responses were rarely >50%.

title: Effect of placebo substitution during long-term betamethasone valerate aerosol treatment in asthmatic children.
abstract: Ten children with severe asthma, who had been well controlled on maintenance betamethasone valerate aerosol for an average of 11 months, were given placebo aerosols without their knowledge. The period of placebo substitution was campared with one 28-day period of betamethasone valerate therapy beforehand, and two 28-day periods afterwards. Symptoms were increased during the placebo period, and patients did not return to their previous well-controlled state until the second month after reinstitution of therapy. Changes in the means of twice-daily peak expiratory flow readings (PEFR) followed the same pattern as changes in symptoms. The exacerbation of asthma which occurred during placebo treatment was accompanied by a widening in the diurnal variation between morning and evening PEFR. In comparison with the previous period, morning PEFR fell by a greater amount than evening PEFR. Standardized running tests suggest an increase in exercise-induced bronchoconstriction and in the Exercise Lability Index when the child was receiving only placebo treatment as compared with betamethasone valerate treatment. The trial provided further evidence of the efficacy of betamethasone valerate aerosol in the prophylatic therapy of severe childhood asthma. As 2 of these children were able to discontinue long-term therapy it is unlikely that this drug causes dependency.

screening.rationale: Within-subject covert placebo substitution examined clinical and physiological changes when active inhaled steroid was replaced by placebo, testing the causal effect of placebo/absence of treatment.

classification.summary: Covertly substituted placebo aerosol for betamethasone in ten children with severe asthma and found increased symptoms, greater diurnal PEFR variation, and reduced morning PEFR during the placebo period, with recovery after reinstitution of therapy.
classification.key_finding: Placebo substitution produced clinically significant worsening of symptoms and objective PEFR, with delayed return to baseline after resuming betamethasone.

title: Acupuncture and placebo: Effects on delaying the terminating response to a painful stimulus.
abstract: An experiment was performed to determine whether needles inserted into appropriate acupuncture points could delay onset of a pain-terminating response more than needles inserted as placebos into inappropriate points could. A heat source contained in a modified Hardy-Wolff-Goodell dolorimeter was used as a stimulus to produce pain on the posterolateral aspects of the left forearms of volunteer subjects. Subjects pressed a switch as soon as pain was experienced, and the latency between stimulus onset and response was measured to the nearest hundredth of a second. Response latencies were recorded before and after needling, which included electrical stimulation. Needles placed in specific acupuncture points called Ho-Ku and Wai-Kaun delayed onset of the pain-terminating response slightly more than needles inserted as placebos. Even with needles in appropriate acupuncture points, analgesia was slight and subjects still experienced pain.

screening.rationale: Empirical human experiment compared needling at specific acupuncture points versus placebo (inappropriate) points and analyzed analgesic (placebo/sham) effects.

classification.summary: Tested whether acupuncture needles at specific points produced greater analgesia than placebo (inappropriate) needling using heat pain latency; found slight but small greater delay for appropriate points.
classification.key_finding: Needles at acupuncture points (Ho-Ku, Wai-Kaun) produced a small but greater delay in pain-termination latency versus placebo-point needling.

title: Topical treatment of recurrent herpes simplex with cytosine arabinoside.
abstract: A double-blind controlled clinical trial of the topical use of cytosine arabinoside in recurrent herpes simplex of the face and genital region showed no significant difference in the efficiency of a placebo as compared with cytosine arabinoside. The high rate of placebo response (70%) found in this trial makes the assessment of any drug treatment for herpes simplex particularly difficult.

screening.rationale: Double-blind controlled trial that reported and emphasized a high placebo response (70%) as a primary interpretation, so placebo response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Found no significant difference between topical cytosine arabinoside and placebo for recurrent herpes simplex and reported a high placebo response rate (~70%).
classification.key_finding: High placebo response (~70%) with no drug–placebo difference.

title: Danthron/poloxalkol and placebo in puerperal constipation.
journal: The British journal of clinical practice

screening.rationale: Insufficient information (no abstract) to tell whether the trial analyzed the placebo effect/response or merely used placebo as a control for active-treatment efficacy.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported as a controlled clinical trial comparing danthron/poloxalkol with placebo for puerperal (postpartum) constipation, but insufficient detail to judge whether placebo/nocebo effects were analyzed.

title: Commentary on placebos.

screening.rationale: Title and publication indicate a substantive commentary on placebos and ethics, meeting inclusion for placebo science commentary despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Commented on ethical, clinical, and physician–patient issues related to placebo use and clinical trials.

title: Sex differences and placebo effects: motivation as an intervening variable.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title explicitly focuses on placebo effects and tests motivation as an intervening variable, indicating an empirical study of placebo phenomena despite missing abstract.

classification.summary: Examined sex differences in placebo effects and tested motivation as an intervening variable; abstract not available to report methods or results.

title: Naproxen: long-term study in rheumatoid arthritis and "placebo pulse".
abstract: Naproxen is by now a relatively well-known antirheumatic drug, and many short-term studies have shown its efficacy and relatively good tolerance. We have observed 64 patients with definite or classical rheumatoid disease, 27 of whom have been followed for well over two years on daily doses of naproxen to ascertain the persistence of drug efficacy and safety. In this part of our study, patients were subjected to complete clinical and biochemical evaluations at two-monthly intervals. Naproxen was well tolerated, and the few side effects reported were transient and mild in nature. Sequential laboratory studies revealed no significant anomaly. Clinical evaluation showed no pattern suggestive of decreasing antirheumatic activity. A question frequently encountered in the treatment of certain diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis is whether long-term improvement is due to efficacious suppressive therapy or spontaneous abatement of disease activity. We devised a double-blind placebo pulse phase in which 19 of our 28 long-term patients participated in a study within a study lasting four weeks. They were divided into two groups. The first group took their usual dose of naproxen during the first two weeks and a corresponding number of placebo tablets in the next two weeks. The procedure was reversed in the other group. We conclude that naproxen remains efficacious.

screening.rationale: Included because the paper implemented a double-blind within-subject placebo pulse (drug vs placebo) to test whether clinical improvement was due to naproxen versus placebo/spontaneous change.

classification.summary: Tested a long-term naproxen cohort and used a four-week double-blind placebo-pulse crossover in 19 patients to distinguish drug effect from spontaneous improvement, and found naproxen remained efficacious.
classification.key_finding: Found that clinical measures and lab tests did not decline during naproxen treatment and that the placebo pulse design supported ongoing naproxen efficacy.

title: Influence of instructions on expectancy effects in Rorschach testing.
abstract: Videotaped Rorschach instructions from a previous study in which two experimenters had biased subjects for high productivity and two experimenters had biased subjects for low productivity were played (audio or combined audio-visual channels) to matched subjects who then took the free association portion of the test. Biased results were obtained for one experimenter only. These did not interact with communication channels. It was concluded that experimenter-expectancy effects in Rorschach testing are not transmitted simply by exposing subjects to biased experimenters' instructions, but instead depend upon experimenter attributes which may or may not manifest themselves during the instructional phase. Limited evidence suggesting that expectancies are transmitted as effectively by audio as by a combination of audio and visual cues was obtained.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of experimenter-induced expectancy (audio/video instructions) tested causal effects on Rorschach performance, so it studies expectation/context effects.

classification.summary: Tested whether videotaped experimenter instructions biased expectancies and thereby altered Rorschach productivity; found biased results for one experimenter only, with little difference between audio and audio-visual channels.
classification.key_finding: Videotaped biased instructions produced expectancy effects for only one experimenter, indicating experimenter attributes beyond instructional content influenced outcomes.

title: An explanation for the 'placebo' effect of bland ointment bases.
abstract: Bland topical applications, containing no pharmacologically active ingredients, were found to have an antimitotic effect on the epidermis of the stripped dorsal skin of hairless mice. White soft paraffin, cetomacrogol cream A (B.P.), starch paste, and emulsifying ointment (B.P.) were applied for 24 h periods under occlusive dressing to the backs of mice. The antimitotic effect was present at the time of removal of the dressings and up to 72 h after removal. White soft paraffin had the maximal antimitotic activity and epidermis of mice treated with it showed only 23% of the number of mitoses of control animals having no such treatment. Emulsifying ointment had the least activity and in some circumstances actually seemed stimulatory to mitotic activity.

screening.rationale: Controlled nonhuman experiment tested biological effects of inert ointment bases versus untreated controls, addressing causal effects of a placebo-like topical vehicle.

classification.summary: Found that bland ointment bases applied under occlusive dressings produced durable antimitotic effects in the epidermis of hairless mice compared with untreated controls.
classification.key_finding: White soft paraffin reduced epidermal mitoses to about 23% of control levels.

title: Letter: A multicentre trial of perhexiline maleats, beta-blocker and placebo in angina pectoris.

classification.summary: Reported a multicentre randomized comparison of perhexiline, a beta-blocker, and placebo in angina pectoris but no abstract was available to determine whether placebo effects/responses were analyzed.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a drug versus placebo RCT in hyperkinetic children but no abstract or full text is available to determine whether placebo/nocebo effects or responses were analyzed as an object of study.

title: Illustration of a control problem in alcohol research designs.
abstract: Issues of control problems in alcohol research, resulting from studies of a possible alcohol placebo effect, are discussed. These concern how the control response is related to the pre-drug response as well as the stability of both.

screening.rationale: Paper focused on methodological issues around alcohol placebo effects and control responses, making placebo science the main subject.

classification.summary: Discusses control problems in alcohol research related to placebo effects, focusing on how control responses relate to pre-drug baselines and the stability of responses.

title: Proceedings: Pemoline in comparison with amphetamine and placebo in pedo-psychiatric practice.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and title indicates a comparative drug trial with placebo as a control but provides no information that the placebo/placebo response was analyzed as an object of study.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated a 1975 comparative trial of pemoline, amphetamine, and placebo in pediatric psychiatric (hyperkinesis) practice, but it was unclear whether placebo effects or responses were analyzed.

title: Behaviorally conditioned immunosuppression.
abstract: An illness-induced taste aversion was conditioned in rats by pairing saccharin with cyclophosphamide, an immunosuppressive agent. Three days after conditioning, all animals were injected with sheep erythrocytes. Hemagglutinating antibody titers measured 6 days after antigen administration were high in placebo-treated rats. High titers were also observed in nonconditioned animals and in conditioned animals that were nor subsequently exposed to saccharin. No agglutinating antibody was detected in conditioned animals treated with cyclophosphamide at the time of antigen administration. Conditioned animals exposed to saccharin at the time of or following the injection of antigen were significantly immunosuppressed. An illness-induced taste aversion was also conditioned using LiCl, a nonimmunosuppressive agent. In this instance, however, there was no attenuation of hemagglutinating antibody titers in response to injection with antigen.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment explicitly tested classical conditioning of immunosuppression (cue paired with immunosuppressive drug) demonstrating conditioned suppression of antibody titers, meeting inclusion criterion for conditioned placebo-like effects.

classification.summary: Found that a saccharin taste cue previously paired with cyclophosphamide produced conditioned immunosuppression, reducing hemagglutinating antibody titers in rats when the cue was presented.
classification.key_finding: Presentation of saccharin conditioned by prior pairing with cyclophosphamide produced significant suppression of antibody titers similar to drug exposure.
